title: FusionFlux: extrapolation, long-range saturation and physics constraints in confinement scaling
description:
An analysis of machine learning for tokamak energy confinement time on the real ITPA Global H-mode Confinement Database (HDB5, standard analysis set STD5). A random forest beats the published IPB98(y,2) scaling law by 36% in log-RMSE under grouped cross-validation by discharge; under leave-one-label-out the ordering of the fitted models reverses exactly, and the forest is worse than a log-linear power law on all 13 held-out database labels and all 11 physical devices.

The failure is characterised three ways: error tracking the Mahalanobis distance of the held-out machine from the training data, the hard prediction bound of a tree ensemble, and a polynomial flexibility ladder showing that what flexibility costs is the tail of the error distribution rather than its centre. Ordering machines by size reproduces, inside the database, a size extrapolation matching the 1.82x jump from the database to ITER; at that cut the tree ensembles score closer to a constant predictor than to the power law.

Split-conformal intervals calibrated to 90% under cross-validation cover 35% of rows on an unseen machine and 3% across the ITER-size-matched cut, at essentially unchanged interval width.

Two repairs are then built and scored. A power law plus a bounded, heavily damped correction on its log residuals is the best fold-fitted model at the ITER-size-matched cut among the learned models. Imposing the Connor-Taylor constraints instead, which any scaling law expressible in dimensionless variables must satisfy, as linear equality constraints on the exponents beats it: 0.183 log-RMSE at that cut, the best fold-fitted score in the study, with no hyperparameter. IPB98(y,2) was itself fitted under the high-beta Kadomtsev constraint, and its published exponents land on the Kadomtsev surface derived here at a distance of 0.00096, which is used as a check that the derivation agrees with the constraint the published law was fitted under. The collisionless rung was selected after the size-cut scores had been seen. Supplying the same physics as a shrinkage prior rather than a constraint is worth substantially less.

Calibrating conformal intervals on held-out machines rather than held-out discharges restores coverage to within two points of nominal on an unseen machine, and, as the exchangeability diagnosis predicts, fails to restore it across the size cut. The reversal is replicated on 5358 H-mode rows the standard analysis set does not contain and on 3860 ohmic and L-mode rows scored against ITER89-P, with the ranking inverting in both. A locked, digest-stamped prediction is recorded for SPARC, JT-60SA and ITER: on JT-60SA, which sits inside the database's size range, the five models agree to within 15 percent, and at ITER they disagree by a factor of 8.3, with the tree ensembles arithmetically unable to reach the physics answer.

The audit is then run outside fusion twice. On 541 mammalian species records across 11 taxonomic orders, with Kleiber's published 3/4 exponent as the baseline, the extrapolation failure reproduces in full while the ranking reversal does not. On 3599 woody plants from the Biomass And Allometry Database, varying only the number of predictors on a fixed set of rows, the flexible models' interpolation margin crosses zero between two and three predictors while their deficit on a held-out species does not shrink, and the power law wins the held-out species at 4 of 4 feature counts. The extrapolation failure is therefore unconditional and the ranking reversal is not: the reversal requires the flexible model to win the interpolation split first, which makes it the warning sign rather than the hazard.

A final result corrects the study's own diagnosis. Separating flexibility from long-range saturation with a Gaussian process, whose behaviour far from the data is a choice of kernel rather than a tuning parameter, shows the failure belongs to saturation: to predictions that stop tracking the features once the input leaves the training support, whether or not a hard bound is anywhere near binding. A bounded RBF kernel scores 1.948 at the ITER-size-matched cut, worse than predicting a constant; adding a linear term to the same kernel gives the best cross-validated score in the study, 0.112, together with 0.191 at the ITER-size-matched cut and 92.5 percent coverage of a nominal 90 percent interval that was never recalibrated. Models that stop trending outside their data are the hazard, not flexible models. The training-target bound of a random forest is the strict case of that and is active on only 1 of the 13 held-out labels and across the size cut, and the forest loses worst on labels where it is nowhere near binding, which is what points at saturation rather than at the bound.

Two controls bound what the headline depends on. The thermal loss power is one of the nine features and is the target's denominator, so a log-linear model can carry that identity exactly where a tree cannot; refitting every model without it leaves the direction intact and cuts its strength, at 10 of 13 labels and 9 of 11 devices, a mean paired gap falling from +0.251 to +0.051, and neither exact test reaching p = 0.05. The interval collapse and the kernel ordering are unaffected in kind. The sharper control is available in the same file and the study previously reported that it was not: DB5.2.3 carries the thermal stored energy WTH, and joining it to STD5 recovers one for 6214 of the 6228 analysed rows, so log W_th can be regressed on the same nine features with the loss power left in as an ordinary predictor and only the identity removed. Retargeted that way the forest still wins cross-validation, 0.121 against 0.193, and still loses out of distribution: 9 of 13 labels at a mean gap of +0.220, 9 of 11 devices at +0.348, which is larger than the +0.315 the confinement time gives, and 1.081 against the power law's 0.289 across the size cut. The identity therefore carries the unanimity and not the effect. Separately, the estimator the clustered-validation literature pairs with this split design, a mixed model with a device-level random intercept predicting an unseen device from its population-level fixed effects, is fitted by REML and scored under the same folds. It scores 0.264 per label and 0.829 per device against the pooled power law's 0.214 and 0.212, and sweeping its one variance ratio shows the best value it could take is the one at which it is the pooled power law, so the deployment-matched estimator does not displace it.

Two arms test whether the headline is an artifact of the analyst's discretionary choices. Running the comparison under every combination of three of them, whether the wall-variant machines count as their own devices or as the tokamaks they are, whether error is pooled over rows or averaged over machines, and whether cross-validation is scored on all rows or only the machines leave-one-out can score, the inversion holds in all 8 cells. Exact sign tests give 13 of 13 by database label (p = 0.00024) and 11 of 11 by physical device (p = 0.00098). Sweeping the row threshold that decides which labels are scored over 10, 20, 30 and 50 rows, and repeating the cross-validation over ten shuffled fold assignments, leaves both conclusions unchanged. Separately, the distance correlation is checked against its own small-sample uncertainty by permutation and jackknife; the newer ITPA20 and ITPA20-IL scalings are scored as baselines alongside IPB98(y,2), each on the elongation it was actually fitted to, which needs the boundary elongation KAPPA that STD5 omits and the full DB5.2.3 revision carries (ITPA20 scores 0.188 over all rows, 0.191 per label and 0.177 across the ITER-size-matched cut, against IPB98(y,2)'s 0.199, 0.188 and 0.194, and ITPA20-IL is lowest of the three at that cut, 0.165); the measured ratio of boundary to areal elongation has median 1.083 and maximum 1.341, with 7% of rows below unity, so the shape model an earlier version used to bound the substitution at 0.0007 was wrong by twenty to thirty times and is replaced by the measurement; and refitting the exponents by orthogonal distance regression, which places error on the predictors rather than only on the target, is reported as a sensitivity check rather than a corrected fit.

A domain-agnostic module packages the method for reuse on other scaling-law datasets: leave-one-group-out scoring reported alongside extrapolation distance and the training-range bound, an ordered-group splitter, and equality-constrained least squares as a scikit-learn estimator.

The repository contains the full pipeline, from-scratch least-squares solvers, all analysis scripts, the test suite, and the scripts that regenerate every reported number and figure. The HDB5 dataset itself is third-party data obtained from OSF and is not redistributed here; it is pinned by SHA-256 and verified on load.
